# Khaggavisāṇa Sutta (Snp 1.3 (PTS Snp 6))

**ID:** Snp 1.3 (PTS Snp 6)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Khaggavisāṇa Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Rhinoceros Horn
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.3
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta* is the third discourse of the *Uragavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983]. Comprising a set of forty-one verses extolling the solitary life of an ascetic wanderer, nearly every stanza concludes with the renowned refrain advising one to "wander alone, like a rhinoceros horn" (*eko care khaggavisāṇakappo*) [Norman 1983; SuttaCentral]. Its core message is that if one cannot find a wise, suitable companion or teacher, it is preferable to wander alone rather than associate with fools [SuttaCentral]. While the sutta itself gives no indication of its speaker, later canonical texts and commentaries ascribe the utterances to *paccekabuddha*s (solitary buddhas) [Kingsbury 2002; Norman 1983].

Scholars have noted the great antiquity and unique status of the discourse. The early canonical commentary *Cūḷaniddesa* comments on the *Pārāyaṇavagga* and this single poem, omitting the rest of the *Suttanipāta* [Hirakawa 1990; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. This indicates that the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta* originally circulated as an independent, detached poem before the final compilation of the five-chapter *Suttanipāta* anthology [Hirakawa 1990; Hazra 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014].

A full parallel is preserved in the Gāndhārī *Rhinoceros Sūtra* (GF 5B) [SuttaCentral]. Major Sanskrit parallels appear in the *Mahāvastu-avadāna* (I, 357 ff.), where the verses are framed as the utterances of five hundred dying *pratyekabuddha*s [Winternitz 1933; DharmaNexus], as well as in the Patna Dharmapada and Tibetan translations of the *Udānavarga* [DharmaNexus]. In Pali canonical reuse, the entire 41-verse poem is cited and commented upon in the *Khaggavisāṇasuttaniddesa* (Cnd 23) and reproduced in the *Paccekabuddhaapadāna* (Tha-Ap 2) [Kingsbury 2002; DharmaNexus]. Selected verses also correspond directly to *Dhammapada* 328–329 and parallel sections in the *Upakkilesa Sutta* (MN 128), *Kosambiyajātaka* (Ja 428), and the Vinaya *Kosambakakkhandhaka* (Kd 10) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
